newsitem.title: INDIA: Japan says India must tear down investment barriers.
newsitem.headline: Japan says India must tear down investment barriers.

text.p: Indian and Japanese leaders on Monday said Asia's two largest democracies need to build stronger trade and investment ties and agreed that New Delhi has a long way to go in tearing down barriers.

"Considering the stature of the two countries, the potential that each has, the relationship could have been a lot stronger," former Japanese prime minister Kiichi Miyazawa told a seminar on Indo-Japanese relations in the Indian capital.
"It is high time the two largest democracies in Asia had a much wider base of exchanges," Miyazawa said.

Former Indian finance minister Manmohan Singh said: "There is immense scope for expanding our contacts with Japan. We have not done all that should have been done to realise the vast potential...We should think big about our relations."
Japan is India's biggest donor, offering 133.7 billion yen ($1.1 billion) in overseas development assistance (ODA), or aid, in the 1996/97 fiscal year which will end on March 31.
But it is only the fourth largest investor in India, ranked behind the United States, Germany and Britain.

Japan also lags behind the United States and the European Union in bilateral trade with India. While eight percent of India's foreign trade is with Japan, India's share of Japan's exports and imports is less than one percent.
"Economic interaction is excessively dominated by ODA," Singh told the seminar, held on the margins of the Indian Engineering Fair, where this year Japan is the partner country.
"There are a lot more opportunities," Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah said.
K. Yoshizawa, deputy president of the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, said India attracted $2.5 billion of foreign direct investment in 1996 compared to China's $40 billion.

"The big gap does suggest no time should be lost in removing the factors that stand in the way of capital inflows," he said. "The amount of red tape is so appalling that it is critically eroding India's competitiveness in attracting foreign capital."
Yoshizawa said India was handicapped by overburdened infrastructure, including ports where he said shipments take two to three weeks to be cleared, partly because of "cumbersome customs" procedures.
He also cited the need for financial sector reforms to strengthen India's capital markets, and a more aggressive programme of selling stakes in state firms.
Singh, who spearheaded India's economic liberalisation programme between 1991 and 1996, conceded that New Delhi needed to tear down barriers to investment and trade.

Japanese investors, he said, were concerned over foreign exchange regulations, high tariffs, limits on foreign direct investment, a lack of patent protection and labour laws that discourage firms from closing unprofitable units.
He called for a tightening of economic and political ties between India and Japan, urging Japan to aim to provide 20,000 additional megawatts of power-generating capacity over the next 20-25 years.
Yoshizawa said India currently can generate only 60 percent of its peak electricity demand and will need to invest $2.5 trillion over the next five years to plug the shortfall.
Singh also called for the creation of joint institutes of management and technology to provide for sharing of knowledge.

"This bilateral relationship should be one of the pillars of the foreign policy of the two countries," former Indian ambassador to Japan Arjun Asrani said. "Much more needs to be done to add breadth and depth to the relationship."
Two weeks ago, India approved an aviation policy that allowed foreign stakes of up to 40 percent in domestic airlines, but specifically barred foreign airlines from acquiring stakes.
The Tata-SIA plan was sent back to Ibrahim's ministry for reconsideration.
Ibrahim has said India cannot allow Singapore Airlines to take a stake in a domestic airline because Singapore does not allow foreign stakes of more than five percent in its own airlines.

Officials said last week the government was expected to rethink the policy to consider direct stakes for foreign airlines. The Economic Times newspaper said on Monday that the cabinet would discuss the matter on Tuesday.
No official confirmation was available on the meeting.

The Times of India newspaper quoted a senior Civil Aviation Ministry official as saying that the ministry was likely to approve the Tata-Singapore Airlines proposal, but with some changes in its proposed terms.
The Tatas plan to start the new airline with 19 aircraft. The Times of India quoted the unnamed official as saying the Tatas would have to start off with fewer aircraft.
"They will have come in with much fewer aircraft," he said.
